messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Factory Worker
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina, a 42-year-old divorced factory worker who had emigrated from East Africa years earlier, described the event that changed her life as happening in a room that was too small to breathe in. During the torture, she had been held close enough to smell sweat, metal, and a sharp chemical odor she could still not name without flinching; she said the details were so extreme that the memory felt unreal, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her. Even now, when she tried to tell it, it came back in fragments that felt alien and hard to believe had happened to her body at all. What made the memory more dangerous was how easily it could return in the present: the smell of a damp hallway, a particular body odor, or the sight of a uniform sleeve could pull it back with force, and during those moments she would feel her body react before she had time to think. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that belief had sharpened after the torture into the conviction that she could no longer trust her own body or do the things that had once defined her, including moving confidently through work and home.

In the months after she was released, Amina began arranging her life around anything that might remind her of that room. She stopped wearing the kinds of clothes she had worn then, because a similar fabric or cut could make her stomach tighten and send her back into the memory. In the morning she put on heavy make-up, not out of vanity but to feel less recognizable and less exposed, as though it could help her hide from whatever might be watching. She kept her mind occupied all the time, filling every spare minute with noise, chores, and television so there would be no empty space for the memory to enter. At work on the factory floor, where other workers moved close to one another around the machines, physical proximity was enough to set her on edge; if someone stood too near or reached past her, she found herself tensing and drifting away from the task, then trying to pull herself back by forcing her attention elsewhere. The smell of the hot machinery during humid weather could catch her too, especially on days when the weather felt like the season of the assault, and that familiar heat could make her think of the event before she had even realized she was remembering. Hearing related names also unsettled her; if someone mentioned a name that sounded like one she associated with the men involved, she would go silent and work harder at distraction, because she feared her own reactions would betray her.

Amina’s sense that the world was dangerous fed this constant vigilance. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, often stopping in the middle of ordinary tasks to check the door and the hallway, and she startled badly at small noises that would not bother most people. What frightened her most was how quickly her body seemed to know danger; the instant she heard an unexpected knock or a footstep outside her apartment, she felt her heart race and her muscles brace before she could tell herself she was safe. Those moments also pushed her back into the memory, because the same bodily alarm would bring with it the smell, the helplessness, and the sense that the torture was happening again. Then she would think, with growing certainty, that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her, and that weakness made her even more convinced that the world remained dangerous. As that fear settled in, she became even more likely to choose routes, clothes, and routines that might keep reminders away from her.

Over time, the effort to stay ahead of the memory made the memory more present. The more Amina kept herself occupied and avoided similar clothes, the more any interruption in that routine stood out as threatening, and the more sharply the torture returned when it did break through. A stray odor at work or the close placement of another worker could bring back the strange, unreal feeling of the event, followed by the sense that it was happening to someone else and yet inside her own body. Once the memory returned, she would scan the room, listen for intruders, and jump at ordinary sounds, which made her more certain that danger was near. That alarm in turn made her negative beliefs feel truer: if her body reacted so strongly, then she could not trust it, and if she could not trust it, she must be living in a world that was still unsafe. She arrived for help only after her avoidance and hypervigilance had begun to cost her at work and at home, and after her ex-husband and sister urged her to speak to someone when she admitted she was exhausted from never letting her mind rest. What she hoped for was simple and frightening at the same time: to feel safe enough to sleep without listening for the door, and to believe that her body and her life could belong to her again.
